### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“We are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids.”

Ancient Greek

“γεγόναμεν γὰρ πρὸς συνεργίαν ὡς πόδες, ὡς χεῖρες, ὡς βλέφαρα, ὡς οἱ στοῖχοι τῶν ἄνω καὶ κάτω ὀδόντων.”

Meditations XI.18. The archive stops after eyelids; the Greek continues with rows of upper and lower teeth.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “We are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids.”
-   “We were born to work together like feet, hands, and eyes.”

### Attribution notes

Marcus Aurelius, Meditations XI.18. Same family of images as VI.54 (the swarm/bee), but a different book and a fuller list of body parts. Citing “Meditations” without a book number collapses distinct passages into one.

#### About Marcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius (121–180 CE) was Roman emperor from 161 and a practicing Stoic who wrote private Greek notes later titled Meditations. He spent much of his reign on military campaigns along the Danube amid plague and political strain.

### Interpretation

Marcus uses body parts as his example because they cannot function alone: feet, hands, and eyelids only work in coordination. His claim is that human beings are the same kind of thing — parts of a whole whose good is not separable from the whole's. He is arguing against the idea that one could flourish at the expense of others, not against self-concern. Written as a reminder to himself, it is compressed into an image rather than an argument.

#### Why it matters

It sets a condition on any advantage: if it requires others to fail, it is not the kind of good he thinks you can have.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “We are made for cooperation, like feet, like…”?

“We are made for cooperation, like feet, like…” comes from Meditations, XI.18 (c. 170–180 CE), attributed to Marcus Aurelius.

#### What does Marcus Aurelius mean by human nature?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Aristotle and Blaise Pascal), human nature is framed through Peripatetic School and Christian Existential Precursor. Some passages define human nature; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through human nature, society.

#### Is the wording of this Marcus Aurelius quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “We are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids.” Forms in circulation that differ: We are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids. / We were born to work together like feet, hands, and eyes. The Ancient Greek reads “γεγόναμεν γὰρ πρὸς συνεργίαν ὡς πόδες, ὡς χεῖρες, ὡς βλέφαρα, ὡς οἱ στοῖχοι τῶν ἄνω καὶ κάτω ὀδόντων.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Marcus Aurelius, Meditations XI.18. Same family of images as VI.54 (the swarm/bee), but a different book and a fuller list of body parts. Citing “Meditations” without a book number collapses distinct passages into one.
